title: Design Circular Queue
description: Brute force to optimized: a plain dynamic array (O(n) dequeue) versus a circular buffer achieving O(1) for every operation.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Design a circular queue of fixed capacity k, supporting: enQueue(value) (insert an element, returning false if full), deQueue() (remove the front element, returning false if empty), Front() (get the front element, or -1 if empty), Rear() (get the last element, or -1 if empty), isEmpty(), and isFull().

blocks.caption: A fixed-size array, reused circularly via modular arithmetic, avoids the wasted space and shifting costs of a naive growing/shrinking array

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A capacity k, and a sequence of enQueue/deQueue/Front/Rear/isEmpty/isFull calls"],["Output","For each call, its corresponding return value"],["Goal","Support all operations in O(1), using a fixed amount of memory (no resizing)"],["Constraints","1 <= k <= 1000; 0 <= value <= 1000; at most 3000 calls total to enQueue, deQueue, Front, Rear, isEmpty, and isFull"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A FIXED capacity, with elements entering and leaving from opposite ends","A fixed-size array reused CIRCULARLY (wrapping around via modular arithmetic), rather than a growing/shrinking dynamic array"],["Both enQueue and deQueue must remain O(1)","Tracking just a \"head\" index and a \"count\" (rather than shifting elements) avoids any O(n) array-shifting cost"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Unlike a general-purpose queue that can grow unboundedly, this queue has a FIXED capacity from the start; the key implementation challenge is reusing the same fixed block of memory efficiently as elements are added and removed, without ever needing to shift existing elements or resize the underlying storage.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Circular Parking Garage With a Fixed Number of Spots
blocks.text: Imagine a circular parking garage with exactly k numbered spots arranged in a ring. Cars enter at whatever spot comes right after the most recently filled one, and when the earliest-arrived car leaves, the "front" simply advances to the next spot in the ring. Since the garage is circular, the "next" spot after the very LAST one wraps back around to spot 0, letting the same fixed set of spots be reused indefinitely without ever needing to expand the garage.

blocks.caption: The tail position is always (head + count) % capacity, letting the array wrap around seamlessly without ever shifting existing elements

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: capacity = 3; enQueue(1), enQueue(2), enQueue(3), enQueue(4), Rear(), deQueue(), enQueue(4), Rear()

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","State (head, count, data)","Result"],"rows":[["enQueue(1)","head=0, count=1, data=[1,_,_]","true"],["enQueue(2)","head=0, count=2, data=[1,2,_]","true"],["enQueue(3)","head=0, count=3, data=[1,2,3]","true"],["enQueue(4)","Already full (count=3=capacity)","false"],["Rear()","data[(0+3-1)%3] = data[2] = 3","3"],["deQueue()","head=1, count=2, data=[1,2,3] (1 is now logically \"gone\")","true"],["enQueue(4)","tail=(1+2)%3=0: data[0]=4 (wrapping around, overwriting the old 1). head=1, count=3","true"],["Rear()","data[(1+3-1)%3] = data[0] = 4","4"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before using a plain dynamic array (which either wastes space with a "hole" at the front after dequeues, or requires expensive shifting to close that hole), notice that tracking just a "head" index and a "count," combined with MODULAR ARITHMETIC to wrap positions around, lets the same fixed block of memory be reused indefinitely.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A fixed-size array is allocated ONCE, of exactly capacity k, and never resized.

Observation 2: Tracking a "head" index (where the current front element sits) and a "count" (how many elements are currently present) is enough to fully describe the queue's state, without needing a separate "tail" index at all.

Observation 3: The position for a NEW element (on enQueue) is always (head + count) % capacity: this directly computes the correct next free slot, correctly WRAPPING AROUND past the end of the array back to index 0 when needed.

Observation 4: Dequeuing simply advances head by one position (also wrapping around via modulo) and decrements count; the "old" data left behind at the previous head position is simply ignored (it will be correctly overwritten by a FUTURE enQueue once the count cycles back around to that slot).

Observation 5: isEmpty and isFull are both simple O(1) comparisons against count, with no need to inspect the array's actual contents at all.
This is the classic circular buffer (ring buffer) technique: a fixed-size array, a head index, and a count, with modular arithmetic handling all the wrap-around logic.
6. Brute Force Solution
Use a plain dynamic array (list), simply appending on enQueue and removing from the front (an O(n) shift) on deQueue, checking size against capacity for the full/empty conditions.
Step by step algorithm

items: enQueue: if the list's current size is already at capacity, return false; otherwise, append the value and return true.
deQueue: if the list is empty, return false; otherwise, remove the front element (shifting all remaining elements) and return true.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A plain list naturally supports append (O(1) amortized) and size checks directly.
Removing from the FRONT is the expensive part: a plain list requires shifting every remaining element down by one position, costing O(n) per deQueue.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Correctly implements every operation's semantics, since a plain list directly and simply tracks the queue's current contents.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for enQueue, isEmpty, isFull; O(n) for deQueue (the front-removal shift).
Space: O(capacity).

Limitation: deQueue's O(n) shifting cost is unnecessary; a circular buffer (fixed array + head index + count) achieves O(1) for EVERY operation, by reusing array slots via modular arithmetic instead of shifting.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force incurs an O(n) shift on every deQueue. Instead, allocate a FIXED-SIZE array once, and track only a head index and a count. enQueue computes the correct free slot as (head + count) % capacity (wrapping around as needed) and simply writes there, no shifting. deQueue simply advances head by one (also wrapping around) and decrements count, again with no shifting: the "removed" element's old array slot is left as-is, to be naturally overwritten by a future enQueue once the circular buffer cycles back around to it.

Allocate a fixed array of size capacity, plus head = 0 and count = 0. enQueue(value): if full, return false; otherwise, write value to (head + count) % capacity, increment count, return true. deQueue(): if empty, return false; otherwise, advance head = (head + 1) % capacity, decrement count, return true. Front/Rear read data[head] / data[(head + count - 1) % capacity] respectively (or -1 if empty). isEmpty/isFull simply compare count against 0/capacity.
9. Optimized Solution
Use a fixed-size array with a head index and a count, letting modular arithmetic handle all wrap-around logic without ever shifting elements.
Dry run for capacity = 3: enQueue(1), enQueue(2), enQueue(3), deQueue(), enQueue(4)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","head","count","data array","Explanation"],"rows":[["enQueue(1)","0","1","[1,_,_]","tail=(0+0)%3=0: write 1 at index 0"],["enQueue(2)","0","2","[1,2,_]","tail=(0+1)%3=1: write 2 at index 1"],["enQueue(3)","0","3","[1,2,3]","tail=(0+2)%3=2: write 3 at index 2 (now full)"],["deQueue()","1","2","[1,2,3]","head advances to 1 (index 0's old value 1 is now logically gone, though still physically present)"],["enQueue(4)","1","3","[4,2,3]","tail=(1+2)%3=0: write 4 at index 0, WRAPPING AROUND and overwriting the stale value 1"]]}

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: Front() now returns data[head]=data[1]=2, and Rear() returns data[(1+3-1)%3]=data[0]=4, correctly reflecting the current queue contents [2,3,4].

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for EVERY operation: enQueue, deQueue, Front, Rear, isEmpty, isFull.
Space: O(capacity), a single fixed-size array allocated once.
Why This Works

Tracking head and count together fully and unambiguously describes the queue's current logical contents, REGARDLESS of what "stale" data might still physically remain in array slots that are no longer logically part of the queue (those slots simply get overwritten naturally by future enQueues). The modulo operation in (head + count) % capacity is exactly what makes the array "circular": once the computed index would exceed the array's bounds, it correctly wraps back around to the beginning instead.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["enQueue when not full","Writes to (head + count) % capacity, correctly wrapping around if needed; count increments"],["deQueue when not empty","head advances by one position (wrapping around); count decrements"],["isFull / isEmpty","Simple O(1) comparisons of count against capacity / 0, no array inspection needed"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The array is allocated to EXACTLY capacity size, once, in the constructor, and is NEVER resized throughout the object's lifetime.
Rear() computes (head + count - 1) % capacity to correctly find the LAST occupied slot, which (due to wrap-around) might have a SMALLER index than head itself.
No element is ever explicitly "erased" from the array on deQueue; it simply becomes logically inaccessible (outside the [head, head+count) circular range) until eventually overwritten.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

A FIXED-CAPACITY queue is the classic use case for a circular buffer: a fixed-size array reused indefinitely via modular arithmetic (tracking just a head index and a count), completely avoiding the O(n) shifting cost that a naive dynamic-array-based queue would incur on every dequeue.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting the modulo operation when computing the tail position or advancing head, which would cause an out-of-bounds array access once the buffer wraps around.
Tracking a separate "tail" index instead of deriving it from head and count, introducing an extra piece of state that must always be kept perfectly consistent (an unnecessary source of bugs).
Attempting to actually CLEAR a dequeued slot's old value, which is unnecessary work, since it is simply overwritten naturally by a future enQueue.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly naming this as "the circular buffer / ring buffer pattern" and explaining why head+count (not a separate tail) is sufficient state demonstrates recognizing this as a well-known, standard technique.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Design a FIXED-CAPACITY queue" points directly to a circular buffer: a fixed-size array with a head index and a count, using modular arithmetic for wrap-around.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why track "count" instead of a separate "tail" index? Because count directly and unambiguously distinguishes a full buffer from an empty one (both of which would otherwise have head == tail with a naive two-index scheme), avoiding an extra edge case entirely.

How would you extend this to support DYNAMIC resizing (growing the capacity when full, instead of rejecting new elements)? Allocate a new, larger array, and copy the existing elements over in their correct LOGICAL order (starting from head, wrapping around), resetting head to 0 in the new array.

How is this circular buffer pattern used in real systems? It is the standard technique behind many real-world fixed-size buffers, such as audio/video streaming buffers and network packet queues, where a fixed memory footprint and O(1) operations are essential.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: The foundational circular buffer (ring buffer) pattern, a fundamental data structure technique distinct from the general dynamic-queue simulations used in most other problems in this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(1) enQueue, O(n) deQueue; O(capacity) space.
Optimized (circular buffer): O(1) for every operation; O(capacity) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Circular buffer (ring buffer): fixed-size array + head index + count

Core Idea: A fixed-size array is reused indefinitely; the next free slot is always (head + count) % capacity, and dequeuing simply advances head (both wrapping around via modulo), with no shifting ever needed
Time: O(1) for every operation
Space: O(capacity)
Most Important Observation: Tracking head and count together (not a separate tail index) unambiguously distinguishes a full buffer from an empty one
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: tail = (head+count)%capacity for enQueue; head = (head+1)%capacity for deQueue; count tracks fullness
